newsitem.title: CANADA: Newfoundland sees C$20 million deficit in 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: Newfoundland sees C$20 million deficit in 1997/98.

text.p: The Newfoundland government said on Thursday that it forecasts a C$20 million budget deficit in fiscal 1997/98, compared with C$29.2 million in the year just about to end on March 31.
In introducing his 1997/98 budget in the provincial legislature, Newfoundland Finance Minister Paul Dicks said he forecasts a C$10 million deficit in 1998/99 and a balanced budget in 1999/2000.
"This represents new borrowings over three years -- if indeed these borrowings are necessary -- of up to C$30 million," Dicks said.
Dicks' deficit forecasts included contingency reserves of C$30 million in each year, beginning in 1997/98.

The minister expected total government revenues of C$3.36 billion versus current and capital expenditures of C$3.38 billion in 1997/98. Revised figures for fiscal 1996/97 were revenues of C$3.42 billion versus expenditures of C$3.45 billion. The 1996/97 figures did not include a C$30 million contingency reserve.
In 1997/98, 44.5 percent of Newfoundland's government revenues will come from the federal government, compared with 43.8 percent in 1996/97.

Dicks said Newfoundland's total debt is C$9.0 billion, including direct obligations, guaranteed Crown corporation and municipal debt, and C$2.7 billion of unfunded liabilities in public service pension plans. Interest payments on the debt amount to C$500 million a year.

As part of its efforts to reduce government expenditures, Newfoundland will eliminate up to 1,100 full-time equivalent positions from the public sector over the next three years, Dicks said. The job cuts are in addition to about 500 positions being eliminated in the current fiscal year.
To augment government revenues, Newfoundland will be raising fees for a number of services, including marriage licences, automobile registration, mining leases and certain legal services.

Dicks said Newfoundland's economy shrank by 2.1 percent in 1996, half the 4.3 percent decline in gross domestic product originally forecast. The minister expects the province's GDP to decline by another 2.7 percent in 1997, personal income to shrink by 2.9 percent and retail sales to decrease 2.9 percent.
Dicks forecast an unemployment rate of 20.5 percent in Newfoundland this year, compared with 19.4 percent in 1996.
"Our province's prospects are good for 1998 and beyond. Yet, the financial situation remains difficult," Dick said.
Dicks said he expects capital investment in Newfoundland to grow by 7.0 percent this year, after declining by 16.4 percent last year.

Other bright spots in 1996 included Newfoundland's manufacturing sector, which grew for the fourth year to reach C$1.6 billion of output. New home construction increased 18.8 percent, fish landings grew by about 30 percent and mineral exploration reached a record C$91 million.
